blocks.text: Acts presents Paul as identifying resurrection hope as the issue at the hearing, prompting conflict between Pharisees and Sadducees over resurrection, angels, and spirits while Paul is in physical danger. Because Acts’ speeches are later narrative witnesses, they can be compared with Paul’s earlier letters without assuming they are verbatim records or using the comparison to erase differences in Pauline thought.

The division in this hearing portrays real diversity among Jewish groups, but it should not be treated as an exhaustive taxonomy of Judaism or used to make broad claims about Jews as a whole. The narrative focuses on a particular disputed council scene and its immediate danger to Paul.

Acts is preserved in early papyri and major Greek codices, including P45, P53, P74, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae; these witnesses preserve different portions and textual profiles. Codex Bezae and related witnesses have a notably distinctive form of Acts, so individual readings require case-by-case judgment. More broadly, historical evaluation of Acts is best done claim by claim rather than by assigning the book blanket reliability or unreliability.
